## Introduction

Cardiac arrest is defined as a sudden cessation of cardiac activity resulting in hemodynamic collapse. Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is defined as death presumed to be of a cardiac cause that occurs within 1 hour of the onset of cardiac symptoms or within 24 hours of the patient's last being seen alive and healthy. Autopsies may reveal a cardiac etiology, though not all SCD cases have an identifiable cause.[1] SCD may be the first presentation of cardiovascular disease and accounts for half of cardiovascular deaths.[2] SCD has a strong association with age. Men have a higher risk of SCD compared with age-matched women. Although SCD has a low incidence in infancy, the annual incidence of SCD reaches as high as 200 per 100,000 person-years in the eighth decade of life.[3]

Coronary artery disease (CAD) is responsible for more than 75% of SCD cases in the developed world. The incidence of CAD has increased over the last few decades. However, a significant decline in cardiovascular mortality is also evident.[4] Early treatment of CAD is the most effective way to prevent SCD.

Results from studies showed that cardiac arrest and SCD may be the first presentation of CAD in genetically predisposed individuals. Myocardial infarction or ischemia is the typical diagnosis in these patients.[5] Early CAD identification and management of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors are the best strategies for minimizing the risk of cardiac arrest and SCD.

Early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is paramount for preventing SCD in patients with witnessed cardiac arrest.[6] Additionally, in younger individuals with inherited arrhythmias, identifying and appropriately treating the underlying condition can effectively prevent SCD. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator use is the only way to prevent SCD in most inherited cardiac arrhythmias.

Heart Anatomy

The human heart is a muscular organ in the thoracic cavity, slightly to the left of the midline. The heart circulates blood, supplying oxygen and nutrients to tissues and organs. Structurally, the heart consists of 4 chambers: 2 atria and 2 ventricles.

The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body via the superior and inferior vena cavae, while the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins. Blood flows from the atria into the ventricles through the atrioventricular valves, the tricuspid valve on the right side and the mitral valve on the left. Ventricular contraction pumps blood out of the heart through the semilunar valves, the pulmonary valve on the right ventricle and the aortic valve on the left ventricle, into the pulmonary artery and aorta, respectively.

The coronary arteries supply oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle (myocardium). The left coronary artery arises from the left side of the aorta and branches into 2 main arteries. The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior surfaces of the left ventricle and interventricular septum.

The left circumflex artery supplies the left atrium and the posterolateral side of the left ventricle. The right coronary artery, originating from the right side of the aorta, supplies the right atrium and ventricle and part of the posterior wall of the left ventricle. The coronary arteries provide the heart with an adequate blood supply to meet its high metabolic demands.

The cardiac conduction system comprises specialized cells that generate and transmit electrical impulses, regulating the heart's rhythm and coordinating its contractions. The sinoatrial node, located in the right atrium near the entrance of the superior vena cava, serves as the heart's natural pacemaker. The electrical impulses then travel through the atria, causing them to contract and move blood into the ventricles.

The impulses reach the atrioventricular node, situated at the junction of the atria and ventricles. The impulses are momentarily delayed in the atrioventricular node, allowing the ventricles to fill completely before contracting. From the atrioventricular node, the impulses travel through specialized conduction pathways, the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, stimulating the ventricles to contract and pump blood to the lungs and the rest of the body.

## Etiology

The common risk factors for sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) and SCD, identified in population-based studies, include risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), left ventricular hypertrophy, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Smoking directly predicts the risk of SCD. Results from the Framingham Study revealed that people who smoked had a 2.5-fold higher annual SCD incidence than those who never smoked.[7] Results from population-based studies showed that the risk of SCA and SCD is higher in people with structural heart disease and ASCVD. SCD risk is relatively low in populations with lower incidences of ASCVD and structural heart disease.[8]

The etiology varies by age, but CAD accounts for most cases of SCD overall.[9] In young individuals, inherited cardiac arrhythmias, inherited cardiomyopathies, myocarditis, and coronary artery anomalies are the common SCD causes.[10][11] Up to half of SCD cases in the fourth decade of life arise from acute coronary syndrome (ACS).[12] Rare causes of SCD include drug toxicity, coronary artery spasm, and cardiac trauma. In contrast, CAD is responsible for most SCD cases in older adults. Other causes of SCD include nonischemic cardiomyopathy and valvular heart disease. Inherited arrhythmias are relatively rare in older populations.[13]

Results from studies showed that 40% to 80% of the survivors of cardiac arrest had greater than 70% cross-sectional luminal stenosis in at least one major coronary artery. These findings vary with the age and sex of the studied population. Although less than 50% of the patients with resuscitated ventricular fibrillation have evidence of myocardial injury, results from autopsy studies reported occlusive coronary artery thrombosis in up to 64% of the patients with SCD. Other common autopsy findings include plaque instability, fissuring, hemorrhage, and nonobstructive coronary artery thrombosis.[14] Cardiac causes of SCD are classified into the following groups:

## Pathophysiology

SCD mostly results from an electrical disturbance, such as ventricular arrhythmias or asystole. Some patients have an anatomic and functional substrate for developing life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias or asystole. However, many patients experience transient events, including myocardial ischemia or infarction, metabolic abnormalities, and drug toxicities that lead to ventricular tachyarrhythmias or asystole. This pattern reflects an interplay between arrhythmogenic substrates and transient events that perturb myocardial homeostasis and predispose patients to life-threatening arrhythmias, including SCA and SCD.[30]

SCD risk is highest during the first few months after a myocardial infarction due to fatal tachyarrhythmias, reinfarction, or myocardial rupture.[16] Ventricular fibrillation and tachycardia were initially identified as the most common causes of OHCA. However, results from recent studies show that asystole and pulseless electrical activity are the most frequent initial rhythms in OHCAs. Approximately 50% of patients initially have asystole, and 19% to 23% have pulseless electrical activity as the first identifiable rhythm.[31] Blood flow to the brain slows to essentially zero immediately following OHCA, leading to death.

## History and Physical

History

People with SCA typically present to the hospital unconscious, with no cardiac tone or respiration. Immediate resuscitation is warranted in patients in cardiorespiratory arrest, regardless of cause. Airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure must be evaluated during a quick primary survey and addressed without delay. A more detailed investigation may be pursued once the patient is stable and connected to cardiac and vital signs monitors.

During history-taking, patients may experience palpitations, dizziness, or near-syncope before SCA. Almost half of the people who experience SCA report no symptoms before losing consciousness.[32] Other signs and symptoms that may be reported by a person who experienced SCA include the following:

Chest pain, discomfort, tightness, pressure related to exertion

Excessive exertional and unexplained dyspnea, fatigue, or palpitations associated with exercise

Prior recognition of a heart murmur

Elevated systemic blood pressure

Sensorineural deafness, which may indicate long QT syndrome (LQTS)

Relevant information that may be elicited during history-taking includes a prior history of cardiogenic or arrhythmia-related syncope or SCA and a family history of SCD or inherited cardiac arrhythmias.[33] Other information that a person who had SCA may disclose in their past medical and family history includes the following:

Prior restriction from sports participation

Prior physician-ordered cardiac testing

Premature death (before age 40) in more than 1 relative attributed to heart disease

Disability from heart disease in a close relative younger than 50

Hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy, LQTS or other ion channelopathies, Marfan syndrome, clinically significant arrhythmia, or specific knowledge of certain cardiac conditions in family members

The relevant history provides clues to certain high-risk individuals. In those with CAD leading to cardiomyopathy and severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, a history of syncope with a documented ventricular arrhythmia episode, New York Heart Association class III or IV classification, ventricular arrhythmia immediately after myocardial infarction, and previous myocardial infarctions predict high future SCA pulseless electrical activity and SCD risks.[34] A family history of SCD increases the risk of SCD in those with inherited cardiac channelopathies and primary cardiomyopathies.[35] The American Heart Association recommends cardiovascular screening for high school and collegiate athletes, including a physical examination and tools to evaluate personal and family history.[36]

Physical Examination

Physical examination findings in people with SCA include unresponsiveness and pulselessness. Blood pressure and cardiac tone are absent. Patients may display agonal respirations or apnea. The skin is usually cyanotic and cold to the touch. Pupils are dilated and nonreactive to light. Muscles become flaccid, with absent bladder and bowel control. Cardiac monitoring may show arrhythmias, commonly asystole, pulseless electrical activity, or ventricular fibrillation.

In contrast, patients with myocardial ischemia who are not in cardiorespiratory arrest have a range of physical findings. Diaphoresis and pallor are often present. Blood pressure may be elevated or within the reference range, but hypotension may indicate cardiac decompensation. Abnormal heart sounds may be appreciated on auscultation.

A third heart sound, gallop, fourth heart sound, and murmurs may be signs of heart failure, which may also manifest with jugular venous distension, bilateral respiratory crackles, an abdominal fluid wave, and bilateral pedal edema. Cardiac monitoring reveals wide variations in rate and rhythm. Tachycardia, normocardia, or bradycardia may be noted. Rhythm may be normal with ST-segment and T-wave changes or outright abnormal.

Individuals with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) often have normal neurologic function. However, ACS and stroke may co-occur, with patients exhibiting cardiac abnormalities, such as new-onset atrial fibrillation, alongside neurologic deficits, such as new-onset dysphonia or slurred speech. The onset of these signs must be ascertained before deciding to include neuroimaging in the cardiovascular workup. Importantly, people who survive SCA may also manifest neurologic symptoms from brain hypoxia during the arrested state.

Specific physical examination findings may point toward other potential causes of cardiac arrest. A mid-to-late systolic murmur of mitral valve prolapse, an ejection systolic murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cyanosis, a right ventricular outflow murmur of Tetralogy of Fallot, and skin signs of sarcoidosis may help identify the underlying cardiac cause. Heart murmurs should be evaluated in both supine and standing positions during the cardiovascular examination. Femoral pulses must be evaluated and compared to exclude aortic coarctation. Brachial artery blood pressure may be taken in the sitting position, preferably in both arms.[37]
